Around 350 CE, in the time of the Gupta Empire, people in India learned to boil sugarcane juice and turn it into dry crystals. Unlike juice or sticky syrup, crystal sugar could be stored and shipped long distances, and the technique spread both west and east.

Sugarcane was first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years earlier and reached India in prehistoric times. Indians chewed it and boiled it down to a dark paste. Crystals were the breakthrough. Our words show where they came from: Sanskrit sharkara gave "sugar", and khanda, a lump of crystal sugar, gave "candy".

How it spread:

  • West. Persians grew cane under the Sasanian Empire. After the Arab conquests, Muslims planted it in Egypt, Sicily and Spain. Crusaders brought a taste for it back to Europe.
  • East. Buddhist monks carried knowledge of sugar to China. In the 7th century the Tang emperor Taizong sent envoys to India, then under Harsha, to learn the method.

Sugar stayed a costly luxury and medicine in Europe until the 1500s. Then the Portuguese and others set up cane plantations on Atlantic islands and in Brazil and the Caribbean, worked by enslaved Africans. Sugar became the main engine of the Atlantic slave trade. In the 1800s Europeans learned to make it from beets as well, starting with the first beet sugar factory in 1801.
